title: RAG, evals and agent safety
seriesDescription: Topic-by-topic quizzes that follow the backend interview roadmap: language core, concurrency, DSA habits, web frameworks, data access, databases, messaging, resilience, security, testing, system design, and LLM/agent engineering.
description: Chunking, hybrid search and reranking, retrieval metrics, text-to-SQL versus RAG, LLM-as-judge and CI evals, and deterministic agent guardrails.
source: Interview roadmap study plan (Java/Spring Boot and Python/FastAPI)

questions.prompt: Why use some overlap between adjacent chunks?

options.text: So an idea cut at a boundary still appears whole in at least one chunk.
options.why: Right: overlap protects against losing context at the split point.

options.text: Because embedding models refuse inputs that do not repeat part of the previous chunk.
options.why: Embedding models accept any chunk; overlap is a quality choice.

options.text: To shrink the index, since repeated text is stored only once in the vector database.
options.why: Overlap duplicates content, so the index grows.

options.text: To guarantee retrieved chunks come back in the original reading order of the document.
options.why: Overlap does not control retrieval order.

questions.explanation: Fixed-size splitting is simple but can cut sentences; recursive splitting respects separators like paragraphs; semantic splitting follows meaning shifts at higher cost. Tune with evals.

questions.prompt: Users search a support index with exact error codes like ERR_4021 and also with paraphrased questions, and pure vector search misses the codes. What is the best fix?

options.text: Hybrid retrieval: BM25 plus vector search, fused with reciprocal rank fusion.
options.why: Right: keywords catch exact tokens, vectors catch meaning.

options.text: Increase the embedding dimension so that exact identifiers are represented more precisely.
options.why: Dense vectors blur rare exact tokens regardless of dimension.

options.text: Shrink chunks to ten tokens so each error code lands alone in its own chunk.
options.why: Tiny chunks lose context and bloat the index.

options.text: Raise k to 100 and rely on the language model to spot the right chunk in the pile.
options.why: More noise costs tokens and may still omit the exact match.

questions.explanation: Hybrid search is a standard answer for jargon, IDs and names. A reranker (cross-encoder) over the fused candidates then improves ordering.

questions.prompt: Recall@10 is 0.95, yet answers are poor and the right chunk usually ranks 8th to 10th. What is the best first change?

options.text: Add a reranker over the candidates and pass only the top few chunks to the model.
options.why: Right: recall is fine; ordering and noise are the problem.

options.text: Switch to a larger generation model and keep passing all ten chunks as before.
options.why: A bigger model does not fix poor ordering or noisy context.

options.text: Raise k to 50 so the relevant chunk has more company in the candidate set.
options.why: Recall is already high; more candidates add noise and cost.

options.text: Remove all overlap from the chunks so duplicates stop crowding the ranking.
options.why: Overlap is not the evident cause of the late ranking.

questions.explanation: Recall@k is the share of relevant items found in the top k; MRR averages 1 over the rank of the first relevant hit; nDCG rewards putting relevant items high with graded relevance. Diagnose retrieval separately from generation.

questions.prompt: Which question is better answered with text-to-SQL than with RAG?

options.text: What was the total refund amount per region last quarter?
options.why: Right: precise aggregation over structured rows belongs in SQL.

options.text: What does our policy say about refunds for damaged goods?
options.why: A policy lookup in prose is a retrieval task.

options.text: Summarise the main complaints in last month's support emails.
options.why: Reading and summarising unstructured text suits RAG.

options.text: How do I reset my password according to the help centre?
options.why: A help article lookup is document retrieval.

questions.explanation: Use SQL for counts, sums and filters over structured data, RAG for answers inside unstructured text. Many copilots route between them.

questions.prompt: Select all that apply. Which practices make LLM-as-judge scoring more trustworthy?

options.text: Calibrate the judge against human labels on a sample, and track agreement over time.
options.why: Right: this shows whether the judge matches human judgement.

options.text: Give the judge a specific rubric with separate criteria, instead of one vague quality score.
options.why: Right: explicit criteria reduce variance and make scores explainable.

options.text: Swap answer order in pairwise comparisons to counter position bias.
options.why: Right: judges can favour whichever answer appears first.

options.text: Use the same model that produced the answer as the only judge, to keep it consistent.
options.why: Models can favour their own outputs, so independence matters.

options.text: Ask for a single holistic rating from one to ten with no written reasoning.
options.why: Holistic scores are noisy and hard to audit.

questions.explanation: Other known biases include preferring longer answers. Judges complement, not replace, deterministic checks and periodic human review.

questions.prompt: A golden dataset of questions with expected answers or sources can run in CI as a regression suite to catch prompt, model or retrieval changes that lower quality.

options.text: True
options.why: Right: run it before merging and compare scores to the previous baseline.

options.text: False
options.why: Golden sets are exactly how teams gate such changes.

questions.explanation: Add failing production traces to the golden set over time, and monitor traces, cost, latency and drift online, since offline sets never cover everything. Red-team suites test adversarial inputs.

questions.prompt: Telling the model in its prompt to "only write SELECT queries" is a sufficient guardrail against destructive SQL.

options.text: True
options.why: Prompts are followed reliably.

options.text: False
options.why: Right: prompts can be ignored or overridden by injection, so enforce rules in code.

questions.explanation: Guardrails that matter are deterministic: validation, allow-lists, least-privilege credentials and human approval, because model behaviour is probabilistic.

questions.prompt: An agent generates SQL for analysts against a production reporting database. Which design is the most defensible?

options.text: Parse with sqlglot, allow one SELECT on approved tables, run on a read-only role with a timeout, and retry on errors.
options.why: Right: layered, deterministic controls limit damage even if the model errs.

options.text: Block the words DROP and DELETE with a regular expression, then run the query with the app's admin account.
options.why: Regexes are easy to evade, and admin credentials remove the safety net.

options.text: Trust the system prompt's instruction to be careful, and review query logs at the end of the week.
options.why: Reviewing after the fact cannot undo a damaging or leaking query.

options.text: Let the model run any SQL it generates but ask a second model to approve it first.
options.why: A second model is probabilistic too, and does not replace enforced limits.

questions.explanation: Also use idempotent actions and human approval for risky steps, keep an audit trail of prompts, queries and approvals, and respect data residency by choosing regions and providers deliberately.
